newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dollar drives German DAX bulls to record close.
newsitem.headline: Dollar drives German DAX bulls to record close.

text.p: Germany's DAX index ended at a record closing high Wednesday, keeping up Tuesday's bull run, with the sturdy U.S. dollar the main engine driving gains and no correction in sight.
The DAX index ended bourse trade at 3,364.99 points, up 44.33 points or 1.33 percent, just a hair off an all-time high of 3,365.03 points, hit earlier in the session.

"There are some decent volumes there and the greenback is helping, especially with the exporters. The slogan at the moment seems to be -- enjoy it and let the cash roll in," said Josh Waiblinger of BHF Bank in Frankfurt.

Dealers expressed admiration at the market's bullish resilience in the face of some less-than-inspirational fundamental factors, which hardly indicated a vigorous recovery but did quell most fears of inflation.
These included sluggish German GDP data, downbeat January industrial orders, a lower Wall Street on Tuesday and a softer German debt market.

The strength of the dollar at 1.71 marks, at or around 34-month highs and seemingly unstoppable at the moment, was viewed by market players as a panacea for any wobbles, woes or potential jitters in the German stock market.
The market shrugged off worries of unspectacular economic growth after fourth-quarter Gross Domestic Product figures showed only a 0.1 percent rise, up 2.2 percent from the year-ago quarter.

What could have been a double whammy for the market came with further bad news on the macroeconomic front after German January industry output figures showed a 1.7 percent drop, mainly driven by a 25 percent month-on-month drop in the construction industry.
The market took this in its stride and stayed steady.

Wild fluctuations up or down barely raise an eyebrow in Frankfurt these days. "100 point shifts have almost normal. This kind of volatility is definitely not as shocking as it was a couple of years ago," said Waiblinger.
He said it was also possible that caution in the United States could be causing some funds to move to Europe, which would boost the German stock market.
